title: Hurricane Nolo's Slow Crawl Could Bring 2 Feet of Rain to Hawaii
summary:
Hurricane Nolo isn't in a hurry — and that's exactly what worries forecasters. The storm is moving toward Hawaii at only 5 mph, slower than a person jogs, while its winds are already at 105 mph. By the weekend, it could strengthen into a Category 4 monster with 140 mph winds.

People on the Big Island are under a hurricane watch, meaning hurricane conditions are possible within 24 to 36 hours. Maui is under a tropical storm watch. Nolo isn't expected to make landfall, but its slow speed means it could sit over the islands and dump rain for days. Some areas could see more than 2 feet of rain, with 10 to 25 inches more widely expected.

"The time to finish preparations for significant heavy rain and flooding impacts on the Big Island is now," the National Hurricane Center warned. "Life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible."

Nolo's path has been unpredictable. Earlier this week, forecasters declared it was dissipating. Then it took an abrupt right turn, headed north toward the Big Island, and regenerated into a hurricane. It's the latest in a busy Pacific season fueled by warm water and a powerful El Niño. Three Category 5 hurricanes — Genevieve, Lowell and Polo — have already formed.

Hawaii has had a brutal year. A Kona low caused the worst flooding in over two decades in March. A 6.0 earthquake shook the Big Island in May. Hurricanes Lala and Lowell hit in August and September. Governor Josh Green says about 1,290 homes have been damaged or destroyed, with recovery costs near $1 billion — before Nolo even arrives.

Forecasters are watching closely because a slow storm can be more dangerous than a fast one. Instead of passing quickly, Nolo could park over the islands, dumping rain hour after hour. That raises the risk of flooding and mudslides, especially on the Big Island, where the ground is already soaked from past storms. Residents are being told to prepare now, not later.
why_it_matters: As oceans warm, slow, rain-heavy storms can be more damaging than fast, windy ones, and Hawaii's back-to-back disasters show how recovery costs and risks multiply when communities are hit again before they have rebuilt.

background_read: Hawaii is one of the most isolated island chains on Earth, sitting alone in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and it has a long history of tropical storms. In 1992, Hurricane Iniki — a Category 4 storm — struck Kauai and damaged or destroyed thousands of homes, and in 2018 Hurricane Lane stalled near the islands and dumped record rainfall without ever making landfall.

That pattern matters because Pacific hurricanes are steered by warm ocean water and by El Niño, a periodic warming of the Pacific that shifts weather and storm tracks worldwide. 'Kona lows' are another local hazard — slow low-pressure systems that form near Hawaii and often deliver the islands' heaviest rain.

The National Hurricane Center (the U.S. agency based in Miami that tracks and warns about tropical storms) uses watches and warnings to give residents time to prepare; a 'watch' means conditions are possible, not certain. Slow-moving storms are especially dangerous because, like Hurricane Harvey over Texas, they can sit in one place and pour rain for days.

Hawaii's steep volcanic terrain and already-soaked ground make flash flooding and mudslides more likely, and scientists generally expect climate change to make the heaviest rain events wetter because warmer air holds more moisture.

perspectives.description: Forecasters and emergency agencies have given residents days of warning, with clear watches and blunt language about what to expect. That lead time lets people stock supplies, secure homes and prepare to evacuate, which historically saves lives in major storms.

The Big Island is facing possible catastrophic flooding and mudslides on ground already soaked and scarred by earlier storms. With roughly 1,290 homes already damaged or destroyed this year and recovery costs near $1 billion, another hit could overwhelm local resources and insurance.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical (why slow storms are the worst)
perspectives.description: A storm's wind speed gets the headlines, but rainfall totals usually cause the deaths and destruction in slow systems, as Hurricane Harvey showed over Texas. Hawaii's isolation and steep terrain make it especially vulnerable, and active El Niño years tend to produce more of these storms.

If climate change keeps loading more moisture into the atmosphere, storms that stall could become a recurring test for Hawaii's infrastructure, evacuation planning and rebuilding funds. The bigger long-term question is whether the islands can rebuild faster than the next storm arrives.
